entries.4efd39cb9898c1752c1dc3031c0c416e1315b49c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv119"/><title type="x-ms">First Thessalonians</title> <div sID="gen32141" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32142" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Thessalonica</hi> was formerly the metropolis of Macedonia; it is now called <hi type="italic">Salonichi,</hi> and is the best peopled, and one of the best towns for commerce, in the Levant. The apostle Paul, being diverted from his design of going into the provinces of Asia, properly so called, and directed after an extraordinary manner to preach the gospel in Macedonia (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.9-Acts.16.10">Acts xvi. 9, 10</reference>), in obedience to the call of God went from Troas to Samothracia, thence to Neapolis, and thence to Philippi, where he had good success in his ministry, but met with hard usage, being cast into prison with Silas his companion in travel and labour, from which being wonderfully delivered, they comforted the brethren there, and departed. Passing through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where the apostle planted a church that consisted of some believing Jews and many converted Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.1-Acts.17.4">Acts xvii. 1-4</reference>. But a tumult being raised in the city by the unbelieving Jews, and the lewd and baser sort of the inhabitants, Paul and Silas, for their safety, were sent away by night unto Berea, and afterwards Paul was conducted to Athens, leaving Silas and Timotheus behind him, but sent directions that they should come to him with all speed. When they came, Timotheus was sent to Thessalonica, to enquire after their welfare and to establish them in the faith (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.2">1 Thess. iii. 2</reference>), and, returning to Paul while he tarried at Athens, was sent again, together with Silas, to visit the churches in Macedonia. So that Paul, being left at Athens alone (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1 Thess. iii. 1</reference>), departed thence to Corinth, where he continued a year and a half, in which time Silas and Timotheus returned to him from Macedonia (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Acts xviii. 5</reference>), and then he wrote this epistle to the church of Christ at Thessalonica, which, though it is placed after the other epistles of this apostle, is supposed to be first in time of all Paul's epistles, and to be written about A.D. 51. The main scope of it is to express the thankfulness of this apostle for the good success his preaching had among them, to establish them in the faith, and persuade them to a holy conversation. <div eID="gen32142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32143" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32144" type="x-p"/> After the introduction (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.1">ver. 1</reference>) the apostle begins with a thanksgiving to God for the saving benefits bestowed on them, <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.2-1Thess.1.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. And then mentions the sure evidences of the good success of the gospel among them, which was notorious and famous in several other places, <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6-1Thess.1.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv119"/> <div eID="gen32144" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32143" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Inscription and Apostolical Salutation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus, unto the church of the Thessalonians <hi type="italic">which is</hi> in God the Father and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen32145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32146" type="x-p"/> In this introduction we have, <div eID="gen32146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32147" type="x-p"/> I. The inscription, where we have, 1. The persons from whom this epistle came, or by whom it was written. Paul was the inspired apostle and writer of this epistle, though he makes no mention of his apostleship, which was not doubted of by the Thessalonians, nor opposed by any false apostle among them. He joins Silvanus (or Silas) and Timotheus with himself (who had now come to him with an account of the prosperity of the churches in Macedonia), which shows this great apostle's humility, and how desirous he was to put honour upon the ministers of Christ who were of an inferior rank and standing. A good example this is to such ministers as are of greater abilities and reputation in the church than some others. 2. The persons to whom this epistle is written, namely, the church of the Thessalonians, the converted Jews and Gentiles in Thessalonica; and it is observable that this church is said to <hi type="italic">be in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ;</hi> they had fellowship with the Father, and his Son Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="1John.1.3">1 John i. 3</reference>. They were a Christian church, because they believed in God the Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ. They believed the principles both of natural and revealed religion. The Gentiles among them were turned to God from idols, and the Jews among them believed Jesus to be the promised Messias. All of them were devoted and dedicated to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: to God as their chief good and highest end, to Jesus Christ as their Lord and Mediator between God and man. God the Father is the original centre of all natural religion; and Jesus Christ is the author and centre of all revealed religion. <hi type="italic">You believe in God,</hi> says our Saviour, <hi type="italic">believe also in me.</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.1">John xiv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen32147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32148" type="x-p"/> II. The salutation or apostolical benediction: <hi type="italic">Grace be with you, and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> This is the same for substance as in the other epistles. Grace and peace are well joined together; for the free grace or favour of God is the spring or fountain of all the peace and prosperity we do or can enjoy; and where there are gracious dispositions in us we may hope for peaceful thoughts in our own breasts; both grace and peace, and all spiritual blessings, come to us from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; from God the original of all good, and from the Lord Jesus the purchaser of all good for us; from God in Christ, and so our Father in covenant, because he is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Note, As all good comes from God, so no good can be hoped for by sinners but from God in Christ. And the best good may be expected from God as our Father for the sake of Christ.
entries.9c7a47e46faf83273297464c7df5646b97122289: <div eID="gen32148" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Thanksgiving to God. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32149" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> We give thanks to God always for you all, making mention of you in our prayers; <hi type="super">3</hi> Remembering without ceasing your work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, in the sight of God and our Father; 4 Knowing, brethren beloved, your election of God. <hi type="super">5</hi> For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance; as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake. <div eID="gen32149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32150" type="x-p"/> I. The apostle begins with thanksgiving to God. Being about to mention the things that were matter of joy to him, and highly praiseworthy in them, and greatly for their advantage, he chooses to do this by way of thanksgiving to God, who is the author of all that good that comes to us, or is done by us, at any time. God is the object of all religious worship, of prayer and praise. And thanksgiving to God is a great duty, to be performed always or constantly; even when we do not actually give thanks to God by our words, we should have a grateful sense of God's goodness upon our minds. Thanksgiving should be often repeated; and not only should we be thankful for the favours we ourselves receive, but for the benefits bestowed on others also, upon our fellow-creatures and fellow-christians. The apostle gave thanks not only for those who were his most intimate friends, or most eminently favoured of God, but for them all. <div eID="gen32150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32151" type="x-p"/> II. He joined prayer with his praise or thanksgiving. When we in every thing by prayer and supplication make our requests known to God, we should join thanksgiving therewith, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Phil. iv. 6</reference>. So when we give thanks for any benefit we receive we should join prayer. We should pray always and without ceasing, and should pray not only for ourselves, but for others also, for our friends, and should make mention of them in our prayers. We may sometimes mention their names, and should make mention of their case and condition; at least, we should have their persons and circumstances in our minds, remembering them without ceasing. Note, As there is much that we ought to be thankful for on the behalf of ourselves and our friends, so there is much occasion of constant prayer for further supplies of good. <div eID="gen32151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32152" type="x-p"/> III. He mentions the particulars for which he was so thankful to God; namely, <div eID="gen32152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32153" type="x-p"/> 1. The saving benefits bestowed on them. These were the grounds and reasons of his thanksgiving. (1.) Their faith and their work of faith. Their faith he tells them (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.8">v. 8</reference>) was very famous, and spread abroad. This is the radical grace; and their faith was a true and living faith, because a working faith. Note, Wherever there is a true faith, it will work: it will have an influence upon heart and life; it will put us upon working for God and for our own salvation. We have comfort in our own faith and the faith of others when we perceive the work of faith. <hi type="italic">Show me thy faith by thy works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.18">Jam. ii. 18</reference>. (2.) Their love and labour of love. Love is one of the cardinal graces; it is of great use to us in this life and will remain and be perfected in the life to come. <hi type="italic">Faith works by love;</hi> it shows itself in the exercise of love to God and love to our neighbour; as love will show itself by labour, it will put us upon taking pains in religion. (3.) Their hope and the patience of hope. <hi type="italic">We are saved by hope.</hi> This grace is compared to the soldier's helmet and sailor's anchor, and is of great use in times of danger. Wherever there is a well-grounded hope of eternal life, it will appear by the exercise of patience; in a patient bearing of the calamities of the present time and a patient waiting for the glory to be revealed. <hi type="italic">For, if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.25">Rom. viii. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen32153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32154" type="x-p"/> 2. The apostle not only mentions these three cardinal graces, faith, hope and love, but also takes notice, (1.) Of the object and efficient cause of these graces, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ. (2.) Of the sincerity of them: being in the <hi type="italic">sight of God even our Father.</hi> The great motive to sincerity is the apprehension of God's eye as always upon us; and it is a sign of sincerity when in all we do we endeavour to approve ourselves to God, and that is right which is so in the sight of God. Then is the work of faith, or labour of love, or patience of hope, sincere, when it is done under the eye of God. (3.) He mentions the fountain whence these graces flow, namely, God's electing love: <hi type="italic">Knowing, brethren beloved, your election of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.4">v. 4</reference>. Thus he runs up these streams to the fountain, and that was God's eternal election. Some by their election of God would understand only the temporary separation of the Thessalonians from the unbelieving Jews and Gentiles in their conversion; but this was according to the <hi type="italic">eternal purpose of him who worketh all things according to the counsel of his own will,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Eph. i. 11</reference>. Speaking of their election, he calls them, <hi type="italic">brethren beloved;</hi> for the original of the brotherhood that is between Christians and the relation wherein they stand one to another is election. And it is a good reason why we should <hi type="italic">love one another,</hi> because we are all beloved of God, and were beloved of him in his counsels when there was not any thing in us to merit his love. The election of these Thessalonians was known to the apostles, and therefore might be known to themselves, and that by the fruits and effects thereof—their sincere faith, and hope, and love, by the successful preaching of the gospel among them. Observe, [1.] All those who in the fulness of time are effectually called and sanctified were from eternity elected and chosen to salvation. [2.] The election of God is of his own good pleasure and mere grace, not for the sake of any merit in those who are chosen. [3.] The election of God may be known by the fruits thereof. [4.] Whenever we are giving thanks to God for his grace either to ourselves or others, we should run up the streams to the fountain, and give thanks to God for his electing love, by which we are made to differ. <div eID="gen32154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32155" type="x-p"/> 3. Another ground or reason of the apostle's thanksgiving is the success of his ministry among them. He was thankful on his own account as well as theirs, that he had not laboured in vain. He had the seal and evidence of his apostleship hereby, and great encouragement in his labours and sufferings. Their ready acceptance and entertainment of the gospel he preached to them were an evidence of their being elected and beloved of God. It was in this way that he knew their election. It is true he had been in the third heavens; but he had not searched the records of eternity, and found their election there, but knew this by the success of the gospel among them (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">v. 5</reference>), and he takes notice with thankfulness, (1.) That the gospel came to them also not in word only, but in power; they not only heard the sound of it, but submitted to the power of it. It did not merely tickle the ear and please the fancy, not merely fill their heads with notions and amuse their minds for awhile, but it affected their hearts: a divine power went along with it for convincing their consciences and amending their lives. Note, By this we may know our election, if we not only speak of the things of God by rote as parrots, but feel the influence of these things in our hearts, mortifying our lusts, weaning us from the world, and raising us up to heavenly things. (2.) It came in the Holy Ghost, that is, with the powerful energy of the divine Spirit. Note, Wherever the gospel comes in power, it is to be attributed to the operation of the Holy Ghost; and unless the Spirit of God accompany the word of God, to render it effectual by his power, it will be to us but as a dead letter; and the letter killeth, it is the Spirit that giveth life. (3.) The gospel came to them in much assurance. Thus did they entertain it by the power of the Holy Ghost. They were fully convinced of the truth of it, so as not to be easily shaken in mind by objections and doubts; they were willing to leave all for Christ, and to venture their souls and everlasting condition upon the verity of the gospel revelation. The word was not to them, like the sentiments of some philosophers about matters of opinion and doubtful speculation, but the object of their faith and assurance. Their <hi type="italic">faith was the evidence of things not seen;</hi> and the Thessalonians thus knew what manner of men the apostle and his fellow-labourers were among them, and what they did for their sake, and with what good success.
entries.b107e72454ec496c52b64d3b3606776fedad692e: <div eID="gen32155" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Evidence of the Apostle's Success. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And ye became followers of us, and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Ghost: <hi type="super">7</hi> So that ye were ensamples to all that believe in Macedonia and Achaia. <hi type="super">8</hi> For from you sounded out the word of the Lord not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith to God-ward is spread abroad; so that we need not to speak any thing. <hi type="super">9</hi> For they themselves show of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God; <hi type="super">10</hi> And to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Jesus, which delivered us from the wrath to come. <div eID="gen32156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32157" type="x-p"/> In these words we have the evidence of the apostle's success among the Thessalonians, which was notorious and famous in several places. For, <div eID="gen32157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32158" type="x-p"/> I. They were careful in their holy conversation to imitate the good examples of the apostles and ministers of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">v. 6</reference>. As the apostle took care to demean himself well, not only for his own credit's sake, but for the benefit of others, by a conversation suitable to his doctrine, that he might not pull down with one hand what he built up with the other, so the Thessalonians, who observed what manner of men they were among them, how their preaching and living were all of a piece, showed a conscientious care to be followers of them, or to imitate their good example. Herein they became also followers of the Lord, who is the perfect example we must strive to imitate; and we should be followers of others no further than they are followers of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1 Co. xi. 1</reference>. The Thessalonians acted thus, notwithstanding their affliction, that much affliction which the apostles and themselves also were exposed to. They were willing to share in the sufferings that attended the embracing and professing of Christianity. They entertained the gospel, notwithstanding the troubles and hardships which attended the preachers and professors of it too. Perhaps this made the word more precious, being dear—bought; and the examples of the apostles shone very bright under their afflictions; so that the Thessalonians embraced the word cheerfully, and followed the example of the suffering apostles joyfully, <hi type="italic">with joy in the Holy Ghost</hi>—such solid and spiritual and lasting joy as the Holy Ghost is the author of, who, when our afflictions abound, makes our consolations much more to abound. <div eID="gen32158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32159" type="x-p"/> II. Their zeal prevailed to such a degree that they were themselves examples to all about them, <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.7-1Thess.1.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen32159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32160" type="x-p"/> 1. Their example was very effectual to make good impressions upon many others. They were <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">typoi</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">stamps,</hi> or instruments to make impression with. They had themselves received good impressions from the preaching and conversation of the apostles, and they made good impressions, and their conversation had an influence upon others. Note, Christians should be so good as by their example to influence others. <div eID="gen32160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32161" type="x-p"/> 2. It was very extensive, and reached beyond the confines of Thessalonica, even to the believers of all Macedonia, and further, in Achaia; the Philippians, and others who received the gospel before the Thessalonians, were edified by their example. Note, Some who were last hired into the vineyard may sometimes outstrip those who come in before them, and become examples to them. <div eID="gen32161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32162" type="x-p"/> 3. It was very famous. The word of the Lord, or its wonderful effects upon the Thessalonians, sounded, or was famous and well known, in the regions round about that city, and <hi type="italic">in every place;</hi> not strictly every where, but here and there, up and down in the world: so that, from the good success of the gospel among them, many others were encouraged to entertain it, and to be willing, when called, to suffer for it. Their faith was spread abroad. (1.) The readiness of their faith was famed abroad. These Thessalonians embraced the gospel as soon as it was preached to them; so that every body took notice what manner of entering in among them the apostles had, that there were no such delays as at Philippi, where it was a great while before much good was done. (2.) The effects of their faith were famous. [1.] They quitted their idolatry; they turned from their idols, and abandoned all the false worship they had been educated in. [2.] They gave themselves up to God, to the living and true God, and devoted themselves to his service. [3.] They set themselves to wait for the Son of God from heaven, <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.10">v. 10</reference>. And this is one of the peculiarities of our holy religion, to wait for Christ's second coming, as those who believe he will come and hope he will come to our joy. The believers under the Old Testament waited for the coming of the Messiah, and believers now wait for his second coming; he is yet to come. And there is good reason to believe he will come, because God has raised him from the dead, which is full assurance unto all men that he will come to judgment, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Acts xvii. 31</reference>. And there is good reason to hope and wait for his coming, because he has delivered us from the wrath to come. He came to purchase salvation, and will, when he comes again, bring salvation with him, full and final deliverance from sin, and death, and hell, from that wrath which is yet to come upon unbelievers, and which, when it has once come, will be yet to come, because it is <hi type="italic">everlasting fire</hi> prepared for the devil and his angels, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.41">Mt. xxv. 41</reference>.  <chapter eID="1Thess.1"/> <div eID="gen32162" type="x-p"/>

entries.b428d34480c79aa66fcb3e98707862cbad498e98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17920"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen36574" type="x-p"/> The AUTHENTICITY of this Epistle is attested by Irenæus [Against Heresies, 5.6.1], quoting <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>; Clement of Alexandria [The Instructor, 1.88], quoting <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.7">1Th 2:7</reference>; Tertullian [On the Resurrection of the Flesh, 24], quoting <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.1">1Th 5:1</reference>; Caius in Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History [6.20]; Origen [Against Celsus, 3].<div eID="gen36574" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36573" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The OBJECT OF THE EPISTLE.--</hi>Thessalonica was at this time capital of the Roman second district of Macedonia [Livy, Histories, 45.29]. It lay on the bay of Therme, and has always been, and still is, under its modern name Saloniki, a place of considerable commerce. After his imprisonment and scourging at Philippi, Paul (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1Th 2:2</reference>) passed on to Thessalonica; and in company with Silas (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.1-Acts.17.9">Ac 17:1-9</reference>) and Timotheus (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.3">Ac 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.14">17:14</reference>, compare with <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.1">1Th 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.6">3:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.1">2Th 1:1</reference>) founded the Church there. The Jews, as a body, rejected the Gospel when preached for three successive sabbaths (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>); but some few "believed and consorted with Paul and Silas, and of the devout (that is, proselytes to Judaism) Greeks a great multitude, and of the chief women not a few." The believers received the word joyfully, notwithstanding trials and persecutions (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">1Th 1:6</reference>; 2:13) from their own countrymen and from the Jews (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.14-1Thess.2.16">1Th 2:14-16</reference>). His stay at Thessalonica was doubtless not limited to the three weeks in which were the three sabbaths specified in <reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>; for his laboring there with his hands for his support (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>), his receiving supplies there more than once from Philippi (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.16">Php 4:16</reference>), his making many converts from the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference>; and as two oldest manuscripts read, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.4">Ac 17:4</reference>, "of the devout and of the Greeks a great multitude," <reference osisRef="Acts.17.4">Ac 17:4</reference>), and his appointing ministers--all imply a longer residence. Probably as at Pisidian Antioch (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">Ac 13:46</reference>), at Corinth (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.6">Ac 18:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.7">7</reference>), and at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.8">Ac 19:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.9">9</reference>), having preached the Gospel to the Jews, when they rejected it, he turned to the Gentiles. He probably thenceforth held the Christian meetings in the house of Jason (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.5">Ac 17:5</reference>), perhaps "the kinsman" of Paul mentioned in <reference osisRef="Rom.16.21">Ro 16:21</reference>. His great subject of teaching to them seems to have been the coming and kingdom of Christ, as we may infer from <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.10">1Th 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.19">2:12, 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13-2Cor.4.18">4:13-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.11">5:1-11</reference>, 23, 24; and that they should walk worthy of it (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.12">1Th 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>). And it is an undesigned coincidence between the two Epistles and <reference osisRef="Acts.17.5">Ac 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.9">9</reference>, that the very charge which the assailants of Jason's house brought against him and other brethren was, "These do contrary to the decrees of Cæsar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus." As in the case of the Lord Jesus Himself (Joh 18:33-37; 19:12; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Mt 26:64</reference>), they perverted the doctrine of the coming kingdom of Christ into a ground for the charge of treason against Cæsar. The result was, Paul and Silas were obliged to flee under the cover of night to Berea; Timothy had probably preceded him (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.10">Ac 17:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.14">14</reference>). But the Church had been planted, and ministers appointed; nay, more, they virtually became missionaries themselves for which they possessed facilities in the extensive commerce of their city, and both by word and example were extending the Gospel in Macedonia, Achaia, and elsewhere (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.7">1Th 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>). From Berea, also. Paul, after having planted a Scripture-loving Church, was obliged to flee by the Thessalonian Jews who followed him thither. Timothy (who seems to have come to Berea separately from Paul and Silas, compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.10">Ac 17:10</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Acts.17.14">Ac 17:14</reference>) and Silas remained there still, when Paul proceeded by sea to Athens. While there he more than once longed to visit the Thessalonians again, and see personally their spiritual state, and "perfect that which was lacking in their faith" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.10">1Th 3:10</reference>); but (probably using the Thessalonian Jews as his instruments, <reference osisRef="John.13.27">Joh 13:27</reference>) "Satan hindered" him (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.18">1Th 2:18</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.17.13">Ac 17:13</reference>). He therefore sent Timotheus, who seems to have followed him to Athens from Berea (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.15">Ac 17:15</reference>), immediately on his arrival to Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>); glad as he would have been of Timothy's help in the midst of the cavils of Athenian opponents, he felt he must forego that help for the sake of the Thessalonian Church. Silas does not seem to have come to Paul at Athens at all, though Paul had desired him and Timothy to "come to him with all speed" (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.15">Ac 17:15</reference>); but seems with Timothy (who from Thessalonica called for him at Berea) to have joined Paul at Corinth first; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.18.1">Ac 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">5</reference>, "When Silas and Timothy were come from Macedonia." The Epistle makes no mention of Silas at Athens, as it does of Timothy (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1">1Th 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36576" type="x-p"/> Timothy's account of the Thessalonian Church was highly favorable. They abounded in faith and charity and reciprocated his desire to see them (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.6-1Thess.3.10">1Th 3:6-10</reference>). Still, as nothing human on earth is perfect, there were some defects. Some had too exclusively dwelt on the doctrine of Christ's coming kingdom, so as to neglect the sober-minded discharge of present duties (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.11">1Th 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">12</reference>). Some who had lost relatives by death, needed comfort and instruction in their doubts as to whether they who died before Christ's coming would have a share with those found alive in His kingdom then to be revealed. Moreover, also, there had been committed among them sins against chastity and sobriety (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5-1Thess.5.7">1Th 5:5-7</reference>), as also against charity (1Th 4:3-10; 5:13, 15). There were, too, symptoms in some of want of respectful love and subordination to their ministers; others treated slightingly the manifestations of the Spirit in those possessing His gifts (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.19">1Th 5:19</reference>). To give spiritual admonition on these subjects, and at the same time commend what deserved commendation, and to testify his love to them, was the object of the Epistle.<div eID="gen36576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36577" type="x-p"/> The PLACE OF WRITING IT was doubtless Corinth, where Timothy and Silas rejoined him (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Ac 18:5</reference>) soon after he arrived there (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17">1Th 2:17</reference>) in the autumn of A.D. 52.<div eID="gen36577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36578" type="x-p"/> The TIME OF WRITING was evidently immediately after having received from Timothy the tidings of their state (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.6">1Th 3:6</reference>) in the winter of A.D. 52, or early in 53. For it was written not long after the conversion of the Thessalonians (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.8">1Th 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>), while Paul could speak of himself as only taken from them for a short season (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.17">1Th 2:17</reference>). Thus this Epistle was first in date of all Paul's extant Epistles. The Epistle is written in the joint names of Paul, Silas, and Timothy, the three founders of the Thessalonian Church. The plural first person "we," is used everywhere, except in <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.18">1Th 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>; 5:27. "We" is the true reading, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>. The English Version "I," in <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.9">1Th 4:9</reference> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.1">1Th 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">23</reference>, is not supported by the original [Edmunds].<div eID="gen36578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36579" type="x-p"/> The STYLE is calm and equable, in accordance with the subject matter, which deals only with Christian duties in general, taking for granted the great doctrinal truths which were not as yet disputed. There was no deadly error as yet to call forth his more vehement bursts of feeling and impassioned argument. The earlier Epistles, as we should expect, are moral and practical. It was not until Judaistic and legalizing errors arose at a later period that he wrote those Epistles (for example, Romans and Galatians) which unfold the cardinal doctrines of grace and justification by faith. Still, later the Epistles from his Roman prison confirm the same truths. And last of all, the Pastoral Epistles are suited to the more developed ecclesiastical constitution of the Church, and give directions as to bishops and deacons, and correct abuses and errors of later growth.<div eID="gen36579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36580" type="x-p"/> The prevalence of the Gentile element in this Church is shown by the fact that these two Epistles are among the very few of Paul's writings in which no quotation occurs from the Old Testament.<div eID="gen36580" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <div sID="gen36581" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.1-1Thess.1.10">1Th 1:1-10</reference>. Address: Salutation: His Prayerful Thanksgiving for Their Faith, Hope, and Love. Their First Reception of the Gospel, and Their Good Influence on All Around.<div eID="gen36581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17920"/><hi type="bold">1. Paul--</hi>He does not add "an apostle," because in their case, as in that of the Philippians (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>), his apostolic authority needs not any substantiation. He writes familiarly as to faithful friends, not but that his apostleship was recognized among them (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.6">1Th 2:6</reference>). On the other hand, in writing to the Galatians, among whom some had called in question his apostleship, he strongly asserts it in the superscription. An undesigned propriety in the Epistles, evincing genuineness.<div eID="gen36582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Silvanus--</hi>a "chief man among the brethren" (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.22">Ac 15:22</reference>), and a "prophet" (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.32">Ac 15:32</reference>), and one of the deputies who carried the decree of the Jerusalem council to Antioch. His age and position cause him to be placed before "Timothy," then a youth (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.1">Ac 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>). Silvanus (the Gentile expanded form of "Silas") is called in <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.12">1Pe 5:12</reference>, "a faithful brother" (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.19">2Co 1:19</reference>). They both aided in planting the Thessalonian Church, and are therefore included in the address. This, the first of Paul's Epistles, as being written before various evils crept into the churches, is without the censures found in other Epistles. So realizing was their Christian faith, that they were able hourly to look for the Lord Jesus.<div eID="gen36583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the church--</hi>not merely as in the Epistles to Romans, Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, "to the saints," or "the faithful at Thessalonica." Though as yet they do not seem to have had the final Church organization under permanent "bishops" and deacons, which appears in the later Epistles (See on <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.1">1</reference> and 2 Timothy). Yet he designates them by the honorable term "Church," implying their status as not merely isolated believers, but a corporate body with spiritual rulers (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.2">Ga 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen36584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>implying vital union.<div eID="gen36585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God the Father--</hi>This marks that they were no longer heathen.<div eID="gen36586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>This marks that they were not Jews, but Christians.<div eID="gen36587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace be unto you, and peace--</hi>that ye may have in God that favor and peace which men withhold [Anselm]. This is the salutation in all the Epistles of Paul, except the three pastoral ones, which have "grace, mercy, and peace." Some of the oldest manuscripts support, others omit the clause following, "from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." It may have crept in from <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">1Co 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2Co 1:2</reference>. <div eID="gen36588" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e3ef7276e413c82ac2e56321bef323261e16324: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17921"/><div sID="gen36589" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17921"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Ro 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.3">2Ti 1:3</reference>.) The structure of the sentences in this and the following verses, each successive sentence repeating with greater fulness the preceding, characteristically marks Paul's abounding love and thankfulness in respect to his converts, as if he were seeking by words heaped on words to convey some idea of his exuberant feelings towards them.<div eID="gen36589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We--</hi>I, Silvanus, and Timotheus. <reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Ro 1:9</reference> supports Alford in translating, "making mention of you in our prayers without ceasing" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>). Thus, "without ceasing," in the second clause, answers in parallelism to "always," in the first. <div eID="gen36590" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9f7c2084e8aede9eaa678416b8dfbc5df87bd3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17922"/><div sID="gen36591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17922"/><hi type="bold">3. work of faith--</hi>the working reality of your faith; its alacrity in receiving the truth, and in evincing itself by its fruits. Not an otiose assent; but a realizing, working faith; not "in word only," but in one continuous chain of "work" (singular, not plural, works), <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5-1Thess.1.10">1Th 1:5-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.22">Jas 2:22</reference>. So "the work of faith" in <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.11">2Th 1:11</reference> implies its perfect development (compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.4">Jas 1:4</reference>). The other governing substantives similarly mark respectively the characteristic manifestation of the grace which follows each in the genitive. Faith, love, and hope, are the three great Christian graces (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labour of love--</hi>The Greek implies toil, or troublesome labor, which we are stimulated by love to bear (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Re 2:2</reference>). For instances of self-denying labors of love, see <reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Ac 20:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.12">Ro 16:12</reference>. Not here ministerial labors. Those who shun trouble for others, love little (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">He 6:10</reference>).<div eID="gen36592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36593" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>Translate, "endurance of hope"; the persevering endurance of trials which flows from "hope." <reference osisRef="Rom.15.4">Ro 15:4</reference> shows that "patience" also nourishes "hope."<div eID="gen36593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hope in our Lord Jesus--</hi>literally, "hope of our Lord Jesus," namely, of His coming (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.10">1Th 1:10</reference>): a hope that looked forward beyond all present things for the manifestation of Christ.<div eID="gen36594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the sight of God and our Father--</hi>Your "faith, hope, and love" were not merely such as would pass for genuine before men, but "in the sight of God," the Searcher of hearts [Gomarus]. Things are really what they are before God. Bengel takes this clause with "remembering." Whenever we pray, we remember before God your faith, hope, and love. But its separation from "remembering" in the order, and its connection with "your ... faith," &c., make me to prefer the former view.<div eID="gen36595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and, &c.--</hi>The Greek implies, "in the sight of Him who is [at once] God and our Father." <div eID="gen36596" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb9ad8c7b8820c5eeb184e993974bcfdab193d52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17923"/><div sID="gen36597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17923"/><hi type="bold">4. Knowing--</hi>Forasmuch as we know.<div eID="gen36597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your election of God--</hi>The Greek is rather, "beloved by God"; so <reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Ro 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>. "Your election" means that God has elected you as individual believers to eternal life (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Ro 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.12">Col 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen36598" type="x-p"/>
entries.558ed9856fe317d37633c6ac5cde72db9168d484: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17924"/><div sID="gen36599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17924"/><hi type="bold">5. our gospel--</hi>namely, the Gospel which we preached.<div eID="gen36599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came--</hi>Greek, "was made," namely, by God, its Author and Sender. God's having made our preaching among you to be attended with such "power," is the proof that you are "elect of God" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.4">1Th 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen36600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in power--</hi>in the efficacy of the Holy Spirit clothing us with power (see end of verse; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.8">Ac 1:8</reference>; 4:33; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.5">6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.8">8</reference>) in preaching the Gospel, and making it in you the power of God unto salvation (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Ro 1:16</reference>). As "power" produces faith; so "the Holy Ghost," love; and "much assurance" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>, full persuasion), hope (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.11">He 6:11</reference>), resting on faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">He 10:22</reference>). So faith, love, and hope (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ye know--</hi>answering to the "knowing," that is, as WE know (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.4">1Th 1:4</reference>) your character as the elect of God, so YE know ours as preachers.<div eID="gen36602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for your sake--</hi>The purpose herein indicated is not so much that of the apostles, as that of God. "You know what God enabled us to be ... how mighty in preaching the word ... for your sakes ... thereby proving that He had chosen (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.4">1Th 1:4</reference>) you for His own" [Alford]. I think, from <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.10-1Thess.2.12">1Th 2:10-12</reference>, that, in "what manner of men we were among you," besides the power in preaching, there is included also Paul's and his fellow missionaries' whole conduct which confirmed their preaching; and in this sense, the "for your sake" will mean "in order to win you." This, though not the sole, yet would be a strong, motive to holy circumspection, namely, so as to win those without (<reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19-1Cor.9.23">1Co 9:19-23</reference>). <div eID="gen36603" type="x-p"/>
entries.32d71b0b5a648413a5faa20a9df608ee6767c619: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17925"/><div sID="gen36604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17925"/><hi type="bold">6. And ye--</hi>answering to "For our Gospel," <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>.<div eID="gen36604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">followers--</hi>Greek, "imitators." The Thessalonians in their turn became "ensamples" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.7">1Th 1:7</reference>) for others to imitate.<div eID="gen36605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the Lord--</hi>who was the apostle of the Father, and taught the word, which He brought from heaven, under adversities [Bengel]. This was the point in which they imitated Him and His apostles, joyful witness for the word in much affliction: the second proof of their election of God (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.4">1Th 1:4</reference>); <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference> is the first (see on <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>).<div eID="gen36606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">received the word in much affliction--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.14">1Th 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2-2Cor.3.5">3:2-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.5-Acts.17.10">Ac 17:5-10</reference>).<div eID="gen36607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joy of--</hi>that is, wrought by "the Holy Ghost." "The oil of gladness" wherewith the Son of God was "anointed above His fellows" (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>), is the same oil with which He, by the Spirit, anoints His fellows too (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Ro 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>, 27). <div eID="gen36608" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcf7ca4ab15696d98b25512071a7ba714ba42ba3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17926"/><div sID="gen36609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17926"/><hi type="bold">7. ensamples--</hi>So some of the oldest manuscripts read. Others, "ensample" (singular), the whole Church being regarded as one. The Macedonian Church of Philippi was the only one in Europe converted before the Thessalonians. Therefore he means their past conduct is an ensample to all believers now; of whom he specifies those "in Macedonia" because he had been there since the conversion of the Thessalonians, and had left Silvanus and Timotheus there; and those in "Achaia," because he was now at Corinth in Achaia. <div eID="gen36609" type="x-p"/>
entries.e04dc65196bcf287dae35dfbdb0c59cd4b40ef97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17927"/><div sID="gen36610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17927"/><hi type="bold">8. from you sounded ... the word of the Lord--</hi>not that they actually became missionaries: but they, by the report which spread abroad of their "faith" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.8">Ro 1:8</reference>), and by Christian merchants of Thessalonica who travelled in various directions, bearing "the word of the Lord" with them, were virtually missionaries, recommending the Gospel to all within reach of their influence by word and by example (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.7">1Th 1:7</reference>). In "sounded," the image is that of a trumpet filling with its clear-sounding echo all the surrounding places.<div eID="gen36610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to God-ward--</hi>no longer directed to idols.<div eID="gen36611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so that we need not to speak any thing--</hi>to them in praise of your faith; "for (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference>) they themselves" (the people in Macedonia, Achaia, and in every place) know it already. <div eID="gen36612" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ba2a1ccdcee9bb8de0d257a8f6a65f82cee5c96: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17928"/><div sID="gen36613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17928"/>9. Strictly there should follow, "For they themselves show of you," &c.; but, instead, he substitutes that which was the instrumental cause of the Thessalonians' conversion and faith, "for they themselves show of us what manner of entering in we had unto you"; compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>, which corresponds to this former clause, as <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.6">1Th 1:6</reference> corresponds to the latter clause. "And how ye turned from idols to serve the living ... God," &c. Instead of our having "to speak any thing" to them (in Macedonia and Achaia) in your praise (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.8">1Th 1:8</reference>), "they themselves (have the start of us in speaking of you, and) announce concerning (so the Greek of 'show of' means) us, what manner of (how effectual an) entrance we had unto you" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>; 2:1).<div eID="gen36613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the living and true God--</hi>as opposed to the dead and false gods from which they had "turned." In the English Version reading, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.4">Ac 17:4</reference>, "of the devout Greeks a great multitude," no mention is made, as here, of the conversion of idolatrous Gentiles at Thessalonica; but the reading of some of the oldest manuscripts and Vulgate singularly coincides with the statement here: "Of the devout AND of Greeks (namely, idolaters) a great multitude"; so in <reference osisRef="Acts.17.17">Ac 17:17</reference>, "the devout persons," that is, Gentile proselytes to Judaism, form a separate class. Paley and Lachmann, by distinct lines of argument, support the "AND." <div eID="gen36614" type="x-p"/>
entries.59ad713288b6557119e638a0d82663031b0d10cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17929"/><div sID="gen36615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17929"/>10. This verse distinguishes them from the Jews, as <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference> from the idolatrous Gentiles. To wait for the Lord's coming is a sure characteristic of a true believer, and was prominent amidst the graces of the Thessalonians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">1Co 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>). His coming is seldom called his return (<reference osisRef="John.14.3">Joh 14:3</reference>); because the two advents are regarded as different phases of the same coming; and the second coming shall have features altogether new connected with it, so that it will not be a mere repetition of the first, or a mere coming back again.<div eID="gen36615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his Son ... raised from the dead--</hi>the grand proof of His divine Sonship (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen36616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered--</hi>rather as Greek, "who delivereth us." Christ has once for all redeemed us; He is our Deliverer ALWAYS.<div eID="gen36617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrath to come--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.9">1Th 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.6">Col 3:6</reference>). <chapter eID="1Thess.1"/>

entries.c387ac5e018c9b25df18144f73d35de07bc1aeb4: <div eID="gen51042" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Thessalonians</title> <div sID="gen51043" type="x-p"/> Thessalonica, now called by the Turks Salonichi, a mere corruption of its ancient name, is a seaport town of Turkey in Europe, situated on what was called the Thermaic Gulf, and was anciently the capital of Macedonia. According to Stephanus Byzantinus, it was embellished and enlarged by Philip, king of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, who called it Thessalonica, or the Victory of Thessalia, on account of the victory he obtained there over the Thessalians; prior to which it was called Thermae. Strabo, Tzetzes, and Zonaras say that it obtained the name of Thessalonica from Thessalonica, wife of Cassander, and daughter of Philip. <div eID="gen51043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51044" type="x-p"/> In 1431, it was taken from the Venetians by the Turks, in whose possession it still continues. It is still a large, rich, and populous city, being ten miles in circumference, and carrying on an extensive trade in silk, the principal merchants being Greek Christians and Jews. <div eID="gen51044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51045" type="x-p"/> Christianity has never been extinct in Thessalonica since the year 51 or 52, in which it was planted there by the Apostle Paul; see Acts 17, etc. It contains at present thirty churches belonging to the Greek Christians, and as many Jewish synagogues, besides some Mohammedan mosques. Thessalonica is the see of an archbishop; and is well fortified, being surrounded with walls flanked with towers, and defended on the land side by a citadel; and near the harbor, with three forts. <div eID="gen51045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51046" type="x-p"/> St. Paul, in company with Silas, first preached the Gospel in this city and the adjacent country, about a.d. 52 or 53. Though the Jews, who were sojourners in this city, rejected the Gospel in general, yet a great multitude of the devout Greeks, i.e., such as were proselytes to Judaism, or the descendants of Jewish parents, born and naturalized in Greece, believed and associated with Paul and Silas, and not a few of the chief women of the city embraced the Christian faith. <reference osisRef="Act.17.4">Act 17:4</reference>. <div eID="gen51046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51047" type="x-p"/> As the Jews found that, according to the doctrine of the Gospel, the Gentiles were called to enjoy the same privileges with themselves, without being obliged to submit to circumcision and other ordinances of the law, they persecuted that Gospel, and those who proclaimed it; for, moved with indignation, they employed certain lewd fellows of the baser sort - the beasts of the people, set the city on an uproar, assaulted the house of Jason, where the apostles lodged, dragged him and certain brethren before the rulers, and charged them with seditious designs and treason against the Roman emperor! The apostles escaped, and got to Berea, where they began anew their important evangelical labors: thither the Jews of Thessalonica, pursuing them, raised a fresh tumult; so that the apostle, being counselled by the brethren, made his escape to Athens; <reference osisRef="Act.17.5-Act.17.15">Act 17:5-15</reference>. Thus he followed the command of his Master: Being persecuted in one city, he fled to another; not to hide himself, but to proclaim, in every place, the saving truths of the Gospel of Christ. <div eID="gen51047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51048" type="x-p"/> It does not appear that St. Paul stayed long at Athens; he soon went thence to Corinth, where Timothy and Silas were, but probably not before Timothy met him, for whom he had sent, <reference osisRef="Act.17.15">Act 17:15</reference>, to come to him speedily; and whom, it appears, he sent immediately back to Thessalonica, to establish the believers there, and comfort them concerning the faith; <reference osisRef="1Thes.3.2">1Thes 3:2</reference>. While Paul abode at Corinth, Timothy and Silas came to him from Thessalonica, and hearing by them of the steadfastness of the Thessalonian converts in the faith of Christ, he wrote this epistle, and shortly after the second, to comfort and encourage them; to give them farther instructions in the doctrines of Christianity, and to rectify some mistaken views, relative to the day of judgment, which had been propagated amongst them. See the preface to the second epistle. <div eID="gen51048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51049" type="x-p"/> Who the persons were who formed the apostolic Church at Thessalonica is not easy to determine. They were not Jews, for these in general persecuted the apostle and the Gospel in this place. We are therefore left to infer that the Church was formed, 1st, of Jewish proselytes, called, <reference osisRef="Act.17.4">Act 17:4</reference>, devout Greeks. And 2dly, of converts from heathenism; for, on the preaching of the Gospel to them, it is said; <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.9">1Thes 1:9</reference>, that they turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God. Though some of the Jews believed on the preaching of Paul and Silas, <reference osisRef="Act.17.3">Act 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.17.4">Act 17:4</reference>, yet it is evident that the great bulk of the Church was composed of Grecian proselytes and converts from heathenism. Hence we find in this epistle but few allusions to the Jews, and but few references to the peculiarities of their religious or civil institutions. <div eID="gen51049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51050" type="x-p"/> There is a remarkable reading in the text of <reference osisRef="Act.17.4">Act 17:4</reference>, which I neglected to quote in the note on that place: instead of των σεβομενων, Ελληνων πολυ πληθος, of devout Greeks a great multitude; the Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, both in the Greek and Latin, two others, with the Vulgate, read των σεβομενων και Ἑλληνων, of the devout, i.e., those who worshipped the true God; And of the Greeks, i.e., those who were previously heathens, a great multitude; so that, <div eID="gen51050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51051" type="x-p"/> 1. Some few Jews; <div eID="gen51051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51052" type="x-p"/> 2. A great number of those who acknowledged the true God; and <div eID="gen51052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51053" type="x-p"/> 3. A great multitude of heathens, besides many of the chief women, received the doctrine preached by the apostle, and became members of the Church at Thessalonica. See Dr. Paley's remarks on this various reading. <div eID="gen51053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51054" type="x-p"/> The First Epistle to the Thessalonians is allowed on all hands to be the first epistle that St. Paul wrote to any of the Churches of God; and from it two things may be particularly noted: <div eID="gen51054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51055" type="x-p"/> 1. That the apostle was full of the Spirit of love; <div eID="gen51055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51056" type="x-p"/> 2. That the Church at Thessalonica was pure, upright, and faithful, as we scarcely find any reprehension in the whole epistle: the Thessalonian converts had Faith that worked, a Love that labored, and a Hope which induced them to bear afflictions patiently and wait for the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen51056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51057" type="x-p"/> This epistle has been divided into different parts by commentators; but these are arbitrary, the apostle having made no division of this kind; for, although he treats of several subjects, yet he has not so distinguished them from each other as to show that he had any formal division in his mind. In the divisions imposed on this epistle by commentators we do not find two of them alike; a full proof that the apostle has made no divisions, else some of these learned men would have certainly found them out. Technical distinctions of this nature are of little use to a proper understanding of the contents of this epistle. <div eID="gen51057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51058" type="x-p"/> The inscription by Paul, Silvanus, and Timotheus, to the Church of the Thessalonians, <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.1">1Thes 1:1</reference>. St. Paul gives thanks to God for their good estate, and prays for their continuance in the faith, <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.2-1Thes.1.4">1Thes 1:2-4</reference>. Shows how the Gospel came to them, and the blessed effects it produced in their life and conversation, <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.5-1Thes.1.7">1Thes 1:5-7</reference>, How it became published from them through Macedonia and Achaia, and how their faith was everywhere celebrated, <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.8">1Thes 1:8</reference>. He shows farther, that the Thessalonians had turned from idolatry, become worshippers of the true God, and were waiting for the revelation of Christ, <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.9">1Thes 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.1.10">1Thes 1:10</reference>. <div eID="gen51058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51059" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51060" type="x-p"/> Paul, and: Silvanus, and Timotheus - Though St. Paul himself dictated this letter, yet he joins the names of Silas and Timothy, because they had been with him at Thessalonica, and were well known there. See <reference osisRef="Act.17.4">Act 17:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.17.14">Act 17:14</reference>. <div eID="gen51060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51061" type="x-p"/> And Silvanus - This was certainly the same as Silas, who was St. Paul's companion in all his journeys through Asia Minor and Greece; see <reference osisRef="Act.15.22">Act 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.16.19">Act 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.17.4">Act 17:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.17.10">Act 17:10</reference>. Him and Timothy, the apostle took with him into Macedonia, and they continued at Berea when the apostle went from thence to Athens; from this place St. Paul sent for them to come to him speedily, and, though it is not said that they came while he was at Athens, yet it is most probable that they did; after which, having sent them to Thessalonica, he proceeded to Corinth, where they afterwards rejoined him, and from whence he wrote this epistle. See the preface.
entries.b03c27e6c6ba8d051e8471087c1e2ed634d65afb: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51062" type="x-p"/> We give thanks - See <reference osisRef="Phi.1.3">Phi 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phi.1.4">Phi 1:4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Col.1.3">Col 1:3</reference>; where the same forms of speech are used.
entries.c1f15c524068666ceff44a158a421ea3c6fb1cfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51063" type="x-p"/> Your work of faith - This verse contains a very high character of the believers at Thessalonica. They had Faith, not speculative and indolent, but true, sound, and operative; their faith worked. They had Love, not that gazed at and became enamoured of the perfections of God, but such a love as labored with faith to fulfill the whole will of God. Faith worked; but love, because it can do more, did more, and therefore labored - worked energetically, to promote the glory of God and the salvation of men. They had Hope; not an idle, cold, heartless expectation of future good, from which they felt no excitement, and for which they could give no reason, but such a hope as produced a satisfying expectation of a future life and state of blessedness, the reality of which faith had descried, and love anticipated; a hope, not hasty and impatient to get out of the trials of life and possess the heavenly inheritance, but one that was as willing to endure hardships as to enjoy glory itself, when God might be most honored by this patient endurance. Faith worked, Love labored, and Hope endured patiently. <div eID="gen51063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51064" type="x-p"/> It is not a mark of much grace to be longing to get to heaven because of the troubles and difficulties of the present life; they who love Christ are ever willing to suffer with him; and he may be as much glorified by patient suffering, as by the most active faith or laborious love. There are times in which, through affliction or other hinderances, we cannot do the will of God, but we can suffer it; and in such cases he seeks a heart that bears submissively, suffers patiently, and endures, as seeing him who is invisible, without repining or murmuring. This is as full a proof of Christian perfection as the most intense and ardent love. Meekness, gentleness, and long-suffering, are in our present state of more use to ourselves and others, and of more consequence in the sight of God, than all the ecstasies of the spirits of just men made perfect, and than all the raptures of an archangel. That Church or Christian society, the members of which manifest the work of faith, labor of love, and patience of hope, is most nearly allied to heaven, and is on the suburbs of glory.
entries.8ffa6e32bc0dcc79f21fbb6dea6885acff44a932: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51065" type="x-p"/> Knowing your election of God - Being assured, from the doctrine which I have delivered to you, and which God has confirmed by various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit, that he has chosen and called the Gentiles to the same privileges to which he chose and called the Jews; and that, as they have rejected the offers of the Gospel, God has now elected the Gentiles in their stead. This is the election which the Thessalonians knew; and of which the apostle treats at large in his Epistle to the Romans, and also in his Epistles to the Galatians and Ephesians. No irrespective, unconditional, eternal, and personal election to everlasting glory, is meant by the apostle. As God had chosen the Jews, whom, because of their obstinate unbelief, he had now rejected; so he had now chosen or elected the Gentiles. And in neither case was there any thing absolute; all was most specifically conditional, as far as their final salvation was concerned; without any merit on their side, they were chosen and called to those blessings which, if rightly used, would lead them to eternal glory. That these blessings could be abused - become finally useless and forfeited, they had an ample proof in the case of the Jews, who, after having been the elect of God for more than 2000 years, were now become reprobates.
entries.5f1080b1ee131515b8e175718ff7e744fe4cb470: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51066" type="x-p"/> For our Gospel - That is, the glad tidings of salvation by Jesus Christ, and of your being elected to enjoy all the privileges to which the Jews were called, without being obliged to submit to circumcision, or fulfill the rites and ceremonies of the Mosaic law. <div eID="gen51066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51067" type="x-p"/> Came not unto you in word only - It was not by simple teaching or mere reasoning that the doctrines which we preached recommended themselves to you, we did not insist on your using this or the other religious institution; we insisted on a change of heart and life, and we held out the energy which was able to effect it. <div eID="gen51067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51068" type="x-p"/> But also in power - Εν δυναμει· With miraculous manifestations, to your eyes and to your hearts, which induced you to acknowledge that this Gospel was the power of God unto salvation. <div eID="gen51068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51069" type="x-p"/> And in the Holy Ghost - By his influence upon your hearts, in changing and renewing them; and by the testimony which ye received from him, that you were accepted through the Beloved, and become the adopted children of God. <div eID="gen51069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51070" type="x-p"/> And in much assurance - Εν πληροφοριᾳ πολλῃ. The Holy Spirit which was given you left no doubt on your mind, either with respect to the general truth of the doctrine, or the safety of your own state. Ye had the fullest assurance that the Gospel was true, and the fullest assurance that ye had received the remission of sins through that Gospel; the Spirit himself bearing witness with your spirit, that you are the sons and daughters of God Almighty. <div eID="gen51070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51071" type="x-p"/> What manner of men we were - How we preached, and how we lived; our doctrines and our practices ever corresponding. And for your sakes we sustained difficulties, endured hardships, and were incessant in our labors.
entries.cb7bb01efacbe9457dbe1d0293db73141530bc87: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51072" type="x-p"/> Ye became followers of us - Ye became imitators, μιμηται, of us-ye believed the same truths, walked in the same way, and minded the same thing; knowing that our doctrine was of the Lord, and that the way in which we walked was prescribed by himself, and that he also suffered the contradictions of ungodly men. <div eID="gen51072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51073" type="x-p"/> Having received the word in much affliction - That they received the doctrine of the Gospel in the midst of much persecution we may learn from the history in general, and from <reference osisRef="Act.17.5">Act 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.17.6">Act 17:6</reference>. <div eID="gen51073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51074" type="x-p"/> With joy of the Holy Ghost - The consolations which they received, in consequence of believing in Christ, more than counterbalanced all the afflictions which they suffered from their persecutors.
entries.48e7de7ff6819e95136ada54e889376e981ad469: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51075" type="x-p"/> Ye were ensamples - Τοπους· Types, models, or patterns; according to which all the Churches in Macedonia and Achaia formed both their creed and their conduct.
entries.fc49f3813a4b824fcd44fed067f745e8bc58cd51: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51076" type="x-p"/> From you sounded out - As Thessalonica vas very conveniently situated for traffic, many merchants from thence traded through Macedonia, Achaia, and different parts of Greece. By these, the fame of the Thessalonians having received the doctrine of the Gospel was doubtless carried far and wide. And it appears that they had walked so conscientiously before God and man, that their friends could speak of them without a blush, and their adversaries could say nothing to their disgrace.
entries.ed727b4fc13117e203f09237a6b2b16e13bb37a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51077" type="x-p"/> How ye turned to God from idols - This could not be spoken either of the Jews or of the devout persons, but of the heathen Greeks, and of such it appears that the majority of the Church was formed. See what is said on this subject in the preface to this epistle. <div eID="gen51077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51078" type="x-p"/> To serve the living and true God - The living God; in opposition to the idols, which were either inanimate stocks or stones, or the representations of dead men. <div eID="gen51078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51079" type="x-p"/> The true God - In opposition to the whole system of idolatry, which was false in the objects of its adoration, false in its pretensions, false in its promises, and false in all its prospects.
entries.9c79f9ae761240b4f89ed225ee3ef990616a467c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51080" type="x-p"/> And to wait for his Son from heaven - To expect a future state of glory, and resurrection of the body, according to the Gospel doctrine, after the example of Jesus Christ, who was raised from the dead, and ascended unto heaven, ever to appear in the presence of God for us. <div eID="gen51080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51081" type="x-p"/> Delivered us from the wrath to come - From all the punishment due to us for our sins, and from the destruction which is about to come on the unbelieving and impenitent Jews. <div eID="gen51081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51082" type="x-p"/> This was the news, the sounding out, that went abroad concerning the converted Thessalonians. Every where it was said: They have believed the Gospel; they have renounced idolatry; they worship the living and true God; they have received the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit; they are happy in their souls, unspotted in their lives, and full of joy; expecting an eternal glory through that Christ who had died for and purged their sins, and who shall fashion their degraded bodies and make them like to his glorious body, and give them an eternal residence with himself in a state of blessedness. <div eID="gen51082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51083" type="x-p"/> These were glorious news; and, wherever they were told, prepared the way of the Gospel among the heathen. The mere preaching of the Gospel has done much to convince and convert sinners, but the lives of the sincere followers of Christ, as illustrative of the truth of these doctrines, have done much more: Truth represented in action seems to assume a body, and thus renders itself palpable. In heathen countries, which are under the dominion of Christian powers, the Gospel, though established there, does little good, because of the profane and irreligious lives of those who profess it. Why has not the whole peninsula of India been long since evangelized? The Gospel has been preached there; but the lives of the Europeans professing Christianity there have been, in general, profligate, sordid, and base. From them sounded out no good report of the Gospel; and therefore the Mohammedans continue to prefer their Koran, and the Hindoos their Vedas and Shasters, to the Bible. It should now ever be acknowledged, to the glory of God, that of late years a few apostolic men in that country are turning the tide in favor of the Gospel; and several eminent Europeans have warmly espoused the doctrine of Christ, and are labouring to circulate the word of God through the whole of British India.  <chapter eID="1Thess.1"/> <div eID="gen51083" type="x-p"/>

entries.7762d0540fb7d030e1c2523b9606869b7fb68542:
THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS.

INTRODUCTION.

I.---THE SITUATION OF THESSALONICA.

THESSALONICA was a city and sea-port of Macedonia. It was at the head of tile bay Thermaicus, or the Gulf of Thessalonica, (see the map prefixed to the Notes on the Acts of the Apostles,) and was, therefore, favourably situated for commerce. It was on the great AEgean Way; was possessed of an excellent harbour, and had great advantages for commerce through the Hellespont, and with Asia Minor and the adjacent countries. It was south-west of Philippi and Amphipolis, and a short distance north-east of Berea. Macedonia was an independent country until it was subdued by the Romans. The occasion of the wars which led to its conquest by the Romans was, an alliance which was formed by Philip II. with Carthage, during the second Punic war. The Romans delayed their revenge for a season; but Philip having laid siege to Athens, the Athenians called the Romans to their aid, and they declared war against the Macedonians. Philip was compelled to sue for peace, to surrender his vessels, to reduce his army to 500 men, and to defray the expenses of the war. Perseus, the successor of Philip, took up arms against the Romans, and was totally defeated at Pydna by Paulus AEmilius, and the Romans took possession of the country. Indignant at their oppression, the Macedonian nobility and the whole nation rebelled under Andriscus; but, after a long struggle, they were overcome by Quintus Caecilius, surnamed, from his conquest, Macedonius, and the country became a Roman province, B.C. 148. It was divided into four districts, and the city of Thessalonica was made the capital of the second division, and was the station of a Roman governor and questor. At the time, therefore, that the gospel was preached there, this whole country was subject to Roman authority.

The city, called, when Paul visited it, Thessalonica, was anciently called Therme, and by this name was known in the times of Herodotus, Thucydides, and AEschines. We are informed, by Strabo, that Cassander changed the name of Therme to Thessalonica, in honour of his wife, who was a daughter of Philip. Others have said that the name was given to it by Philip himself, in memory of a victory which he obtained over the armies of Thessaly. In the time of Brutus and Cassius it was a city of so much importance that the promise of being permitted to plunder the city, as the reward of victory, infused new courage into their armies. The city was inhabited by Greeks, Romans, and Jews. It adored many gods, but particularly Jupiter, as the father of Hercules, the alleged founder of its ancient royal family. It had a celebrated amphitheatre, where gladiatorial shows were exhibited for the amusement of the citizens, and a circus for public games. The Roman part of the population was, of course, introduced after the conquest, and it is impossible now to estimate the relative number of the Greeks and the Romans in the time when the gospel was preached there. In common with most of the other cities of Greece, a considerable number of Jews resided there, who had a synagogue at the time when the city was visited by Paul, Acts 17:1. Little is known of the morals of the place, but there is reason to believe that it was somewhat distinguished for dissoluteness of manners. "The females, particularly, could claim little credit on the score of modest, retiring demeanour; for this virtue was in so low estimation in the city, that the place was selected as the scene of the wanton fancies of the satirist." (Lucian.) See Hug. Intro.

The name of the place now is Saloniki. It is a Turkish commercial town, and contains about 70,000 inhabitants. Its situation and appearance are thus described by Dr. Clarke. "The walls of Salonica give a very remarkable appearance to the town, and cause it to be seen at a great distance, being white-washed; and what is still more extraordinary, they are painted. They extend in a semi-circular manner from the sea, enclosing the whole of the buildings within a peribolus, whose circuit is five or six miles; but a great part of the space within the walls is void.
